title: Last Day In Florida

jokes.text: Michael-esque announcement: 'Dwight is no longer with us... He's gone, damn it!' — played as death announcement before reveal he was promoted
jokes.setup: Andy gathers everyone and gravely announces 'Dwight is no longer with us. He's gone, damn it!'
jokes.punchline: 'So... He's alive.' 'Yeah. That was him on the phone.'
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection — dramatic death announcement turns out to be a promotion. The structure is solid and the deadpan follow-up ('So... He's alive.') lands well. Andy's obliviousness to how he sounds is character-consistent. Not entirely original — this beat has been done before — but it's executed cleanly.

jokes.text: 'How could I have been more clear? He had a massive stroke of good fortune and he is now in a better place.'
jokes.setup: Office workers point out Andy's announcement sounded like Dwight died.
jokes.punchline: Andy doubles down with 'massive stroke of good fortune' and 'better place' — both phrases that also sound like death euphemisms — completely unaware.
jokes.explanation: This is the better half of the opening joke. The escalation — Andy trying to clarify and only making it worse with MORE death-coded language ('massive stroke,' 'better place') — is genuinely clever double-meaning wordplay. The character work is strong: Andy is blissfully unaware, which is pitch-perfect. Tight economy, strong structure.

jokes.text: 'If Dwight's not coming back, does that mean we can open his treasure?'
jokes.setup: Office reacts to Dwight's departure.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's first concern is whether they can now access Dwight's mysterious 'treasure' — a perfectly Kevin non-sequitur that also reveals the office has been obsessing over this.
jokes.explanation: Short, punchy, and very Kevin. The word 'treasure' is already funny, and Kevin cutting through the emotional moment to ask about material gain is perfectly in-character. The joke also sets up the B-plot economically.

jokes.text: Confessional: 'Which is obviously what he would want us to think, making it the perfect place to hide a treasure! Oh, God, I'm Wallace Shawn — The Princess Bride!'
jokes.setup: Oscar is doing a talking head where he's rationalizing why there definitely IS a treasure despite Andy saying there isn't.
jokes.punchline: Oscar catches himself mid-logic-spiral and realizes he's doing the exact Wallace Shawn 'inconceivable' bit from The Princess Bride, and calls himself out on it.
jokes.explanation: Clever meta moment — Oscar is smart enough to recognize his own logical spiral and the pop culture parallel. The self-awareness is genuinely funny and well-integrated: it's exactly what Oscar would do. The reference lands because the parallel is tight, not just a random name-drop.

jokes.text: Dwight's pre-departure warning 'Don't touch my treasure' shown in flashback, followed by Andy's analysis that 'obviously, he wants us to obsess about it. There's nothing in there.'
jokes.setup: Andy insists there is no treasure and that Dwight just wants them to obsess over it
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'logical' refutation ironically proves he is also obsessing over it
jokes.explanation: Solid layered irony — the guy insisting there's nothing there is clearly desperately curious. Character-appropriate for both Andy (oblivious self-contradiction) and Dwight (the pre-planned power move of leaving a 'treasure').

jokes.text: 'I think that Dwight wanted us to realize that this conversation among friends is the true treasure.' — followed by 'That's not Dwight. No.'
jokes.setup: Office is spiraling about Dwight's treasure box.
jokes.punchline: Andy tries a saccharine, Hallmark-movie interpretation; the office shuts it down immediately with 'That's not Dwight.'
jokes.explanation: Solid community gag — the entire office instantly recognizing that Andy's warm interpretation is completely wrong for Dwight's character is funny because it's true. Short, punchy dismissal. Not exceptional but works well.

jokes.text: 'I am dying to know what's in there.' 'Yeah, I know, Oscar. We all are. But nobody's gonna open it. You'd have to be insane.'
jokes.setup: Andy declares nobody would open the box — you'd have to be insane.
jokes.punchline: Cut immediately to Andy opening the box.
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom cut — character says something won't happen, instant cut to it happening. The joke is in the speed and confidence of Andy's hypocrisy. Not original as a structure but very cleanly executed.

jokes.text: 'It's a photo of all of us. Oh, that's so sweet.'
jokes.setup: Office opens Dwight's mysterious 'treasure' with great ceremony and anticipation.
jokes.punchline: First item is a sentimental group photo — totally at odds with Dwight's character, generating a brief 'maybe he's sweet' beat before the dart.
jokes.explanation: The photo is a setup beat for the dart that follows. On its own it's mild — the 'sweet' reaction is part of a two-beat gag. Gets rewatch value because you know what's coming.

jokes.text: Someone opens Dwight's box and is immediately hit by a dart — 'A dart? Are you kidding me? Who would put a poison dart-- Well, I mean, I don't know that it's poison. I just have to imagine.'
jokes.setup: The treasure box is opened after much anticipation; we just saw the sweet photo.
jokes.punchline: Dwight has booby-trapped the box with a dart. The victim immediately hedges on whether it's poison — perfectly Dunder Mifflin logic.
jokes.explanation: This is quintessential Dwight — of course he booby-trapped the box. The dart is a perfect payoff to the treasure buildup. The hedge ('I don't know that it's POISON. I just have to imagine') is very funny in its resigned Office-world logic. Strong character integration: this could only be a Dwight joke. The photo-as-red-herring setup makes the dart land harder.

jokes.text: Talking head: 'Kinda sounds like he deserved it, opening another man's treasure and all. Wow!'
jokes.setup: Someone has just been darted opening Dwight's box.
jokes.punchline: Creed delivers a completely deadpan, morally skewed take — as if violating the 'treasure' code is the real offense. 'Wow!' at the end undercuts any sympathy.
jokes.explanation: Pure Creed. The inversion of sympathy — victim deserved it for violating treasure protocol — delivered with total sincerity, is perfectly calibrated Creed Bratton comedy. 'Wow!' is an inspired button: it reads as Creed being impressed by the dare of opening the box, not horrified by the dart. Very high character integration; this joke is untransferable to any other character.

jokes.text: Robert California playing golf, addressing a golf ball: 'Well, Mr. Ball, it's been a pleasure. Now give my regards to hell! Dah!'
jokes.setup: Robert California is on the golf course, apparently mid-game.
jokes.punchline: He addresses the ball as 'Mr. Ball,' gives it formal regards, then commands it to hell before hitting it — with full theatrical commitment.
jokes.explanation: Robert California's grandiosity applied to a mundane golf shot is perfectly in character. The formal address to an inanimate object ('Mr. Ball'), the diplomatic farewell, and the sudden 'give my regards to hell!' is unexpected and very funny. High character integration — this could only be Robert.

jokes.text: 'All right! Well swung, my VIP VP.'
jokes.setup: Robert hits the golf shot dramatically.
jokes.punchline: Dwight immediately sycophantically compliments him with the alliterative 'VIP VP' — trying too hard to impress his new boss.
jokes.explanation: Mild wordplay that reveals Dwight's obsequiousness around Robert. Functional but not memorable. 'VIP VP' is a minor bit of wordplay with decent character insight.

jokes.text: Robert: 'We are a regular Archibald and his man George.' Dwight: 'I bet. I'm excited.' Robert: 'Trick! There's no such thing. It's not even a real English duo.'
jokes.setup: Robert compares himself and Dwight to a famous duo, building excitement.
jokes.punchline: He immediately reveals it was a fake reference — 'Trick! There's no such thing' — and Dwight had already agreed enthusiastically, exposing his sycophancy.
jokes.explanation: This is genuinely clever writing. Robert invents a prestigious-sounding fake cultural reference, Dwight immediately plays along ('I bet. I'm excited.'), and Robert springs the trap: 'Trick!' It simultaneously exposes Dwight's sycophancy and establishes Robert as a manipulative game-player who tests people for sport. 'It's not even a real English duo' is a hilarious non-explanation. High originality, strong character work for both characters.

jokes.text: 'I just made you look like the Goat of Dover.' 'And that doesn't exist either.'
jokes.setup: Robert has just revealed his 'Archibald and George' reference was fake.
jokes.punchline: He compounds it by saying he made Dwight look like 'the Goat of Dover' — and then immediately admits that also doesn't exist.
jokes.explanation: The escalation of Robert's game — he's not done, he compounds the fake reference with yet another invented thing ('Goat of Dover') and undercuts it himself before anyone can question it. It reveals a man who enjoys the absurdity of his own manipulations. 'And that doesn't exist either' is the perfect button. Compact, confident, and very Robert California.

jokes.text: 'You think you're excited? You should feel my nipples. Boing!'
jokes.setup: Robert expresses excitement about working with Dwight.
jokes.punchline: Dwight one-ups him with a TMI physical revelation about his own nipple state, complete with the verbal 'Boing!'
jokes.explanation: Very Dwight — physical oversharing with complete sincerity and no self-consciousness. 'Boing!' as the verbal sound effect is inspired and makes it more quotable than it would otherwise be. The joke relies somewhat on shock value but the character specificity rescues it from being purely cheap.

jokes.text: Dwight hits a golf shot and shouts 'Fore!' — Robert and Jim react: 'Oh yeah!' / 'He doesn't even care.' 'Don't even care!'
jokes.setup: Dwight hits a golf shot.
jokes.punchline: The reaction is split between Robert's enthusiasm ('Oh yeah!') and Jim's observation that Dwight 'doesn't even care' where it goes — which Dwight immediately confirms with gleeful indifference.
jokes.explanation: Mild character moment — Dwight's chaotic golf approach matches his personality. The Jim observation functions as a talking-head beat. Functional but lightweight.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'This is the last time I'll ever see Dwight. It's a weird feeling. It's, um... What's the word? It's not bittersweet. It's, uh... Sweet.'
jokes.setup: Jim reflects emotionally on Dwight's departure, appearing to search for the right word.
jokes.punchline: After feigning emotional complexity, he lands on simply 'Sweet' — he's just happy Dwight is leaving.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: Jim mimics the emotional language of someone struggling to find words for a complex feeling, builds anticipation, then deflates it completely with 'Sweet.' It's economical, beautifully in-character (Jim's dry antagonism toward Dwight), and quietly devastating. High quotability. The pause before 'Sweet' does a lot of work.

jokes.text: Cookie-selling subplot begins: 'Hey, man. Selling cookies for Jada. Want the same as last year?' 'Would if I could and I can, so I will. Put me down for one box. Don't care what it is, dealer's choice.' 'I'll put you down for shortbreads.' 'Damn it!'
jokes.setup: Darryl is selling Girl Scout cookies and asks Kevin what he wants, Kevin gives an elaborate non-preference ('dealer's choice').
jokes.punchline: Darryl assigns shortbreads; Kevin is immediately disappointed — the 'don't care' was obviously a lie.
jokes.explanation: A tight little joke. Kevin's overcomplicated non-preference ('Would if I could and I can, so I will') followed by instant disappointment at the outcome he supposedly didn't care about is very Kevin. 'Damn it!' is a perfect button. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Toby appears selling cookies for his daughter: 'Knock, knock. Hey, it's Sasha's first year in the troupe, so I'm selling cookies for her.' Darryl's reaction: 'No!' immediately and firmly.
jokes.setup: Toby shows up to sell cookies in Darryl's established territory.
jokes.punchline: Darryl's immediate, emphatic 'No!' before Toby even finishes his pitch.
jokes.explanation: Darryl's rejection of Toby is funny both for the speed and the specificity — it's territorial, not personal (or is it?). The setup is quick and the beat works. Standard but well-executed.

jokes.text: Darryl defending his cookie territory: 'This is the only place I interact with people. Can't you sell at... Your church or barbershop? Or... Chess club?'
jokes.setup: Toby argues Darryl can't claim territory.
jokes.punchline: Darryl reveals his cookie route IS his social life, then tries to redirect Toby to venues that reveal assumptions about Toby's social world ('chess club').
jokes.explanation: The funniest part is the inadvertent self-revelation: 'This is the only place I interact with people' is more pathetic than Darryl intends. The 'chess club' suggestion as a Toby-specific dig is a nice touch — assumes Toby is the stereotypical lonely nerd.

jokes.text: Darryl negotiates territory split: 'You can have sales, the annex, creed.' — listing Creed as a territory.
jokes.setup: Darryl and Toby divide up the office as cookie-selling territory.
jokes.punchline: Darryl lists 'Creed' as a zone unto himself — as if Creed is a geographical region requiring separate consideration.
jokes.explanation: A small but very funny joke. Creed being categorized as a standalone territory — not part of any normal office section — is a great background gag that characterizes both Creed's otherness and Darryl's pragmatism. Very economical.

jokes.text: Darryl's talking head about Kevin: 'All I need is Kevin. Dude buys more cookies than everyone combined, and then some. When I first started selling cookies, he was a relatively thin man. Not a thin man, mind you. Relatively thin.'
jokes.setup: Darryl explains his cookie strategy in a confessional.
jokes.punchline: The Kevin weight history is revealed — 'relatively thin... not a thin man, mind you. Relatively thin' — the qualifier doing enormous comic work.
jokes.explanation: Excellent economy. The hedge 'not a thin man, mind you. Relatively thin' is the joke — Darryl carefully calibrating his description tells us everything about Kevin's past AND present weight while being technically polite. The 'and then some' at the start also gets a laugh. Very well-structured confessional.

jokes.text: Dwight in Florida: 'Oh, what kind of tea is this?' Irene: 'Oh, I boiled some Gatorade.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is having tea with Irene, the elderly woman he's been helping.
jokes.punchline: The tea is boiled Gatorade — an absurd but also kind of logical elder-logic substitution.
jokes.explanation: Very funny absurdist detail. 'Boiled Gatorade' is both disgusting and weirdly plausible for an elderly Floridian. The line is delivered with complete sincerity which makes it funnier. High economy — the joke is three words.

jokes.text: 'Hey Lucy, I'm home! Bobaloo!' — Dwight's Floridian living situation reveal, plus 'It was so busy at the store today. Really good cheese samples. I had, like, a hundred.'
jokes.setup: We cut to Dwight's new Florida life; he's moved in with an elderly woman named Irene as her 'live-in helper'
jokes.punchline: Dwight enters doing an I Love Lucy impression, then his housemate Irene has eaten approximately one hundred cheese samples at the store — a mundane detail delivered with total innocence
jokes.explanation: The I Love Lucy reference from Dwight is slightly inexplicable but funny in its randomness. The 'hundred cheese samples' is the better joke — Irene's total guilelessness about eating that many samples is a small gem. The scene works primarily as world-building for Dwight's absurd domestic arrangement.

jokes.text: Irene's non sequitur about her grandson: 'He's a wonderful swimmer. Shallow end, deep end. He does it all.'
jokes.setup: Dwight tells Irene today will be tough because he needs to call his old boss to say he's staying in Florida
jokes.punchline: Irene ignores the emotional content entirely and pivots to praising her grandson's swimming abilities, with the specific qualifier 'shallow end, deep end — he does it all'
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the grandmotherly non sequitur — completely ignoring Dwight's emotional disclosure to brag about a grandchild. 'Shallow end, deep end. He does it all.' is the punchline because the qualifier is so grandmotherly in its low-bar pride. 'He does it all' about swimming in a pool is a perfect encapsulation of elderly relative enthusiasm.

jokes.text: Kevin interrupts a golf lesson to try to sell cookies: 'Would you like to buy some cookies?' — scene cuts immediately as Robert considers.
jokes.setup: Robert California is in the middle of a serious golf putting lesson with Dwight.
jokes.punchline: Kevin materializes out of nowhere to pitch cookies, completely undercutting the gravitas of the moment.
jokes.explanation: The intrusion of Kevin's mundane cookie mission into the theatrical Robert/Dwight dynamic is funny. Robert's 'Cookies, eh?' suggests he's genuinely intrigued, which is also funny — Robert California taking a cookie pitch seriously.

jokes.text: Kevin sings an original cookie season song to Robert California: '♪ Oh, the springtime thinks that it's the best... but gather round, peeps, I'll tell you the truth / Nothing beats the cookie season ♪'
jokes.setup: Kevin is pitching cookies to Robert California in an elaborate Florida golf setting.
jokes.punchline: Kevin launches into a full original song about cookie season with complete earnestness — 'gather round, peeps' being a particularly inspired lyric.
jokes.explanation: Kevin writing and performing an original cookie-season song is deeply in character — his lack of self-awareness combined with genuine enthusiasm makes it work. 'Gather round, peeps' is a funny turn of phrase. The song goes on a bit, slightly bloating it, but the premise is strong.

jokes.text: 'It's not a scratch and sniff, Kev.' 'I know. But sometimes you still get a little something.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is apparently sniffing a cookie box or cookie catalogue.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's defense — 'sometimes you still get a little something' — is both disgusting and weirdly sincere.
jokes.explanation: Short and very funny. Kevin's relationship with food is so pure and tragic that sniffing a non-scratch-and-sniff catalogue for a 'little something' is both absurd and completely believable for him. Strong economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Darryl catching Toby poaching Kevin: 'Hey, you tricked me. You just wanted Kevin.' Darryl: 'You're new to the game. You learned a lesson today. See you next year, sport.'
jokes.setup: Darryl realizes the territory split was a ruse — Toby accepted the smaller territory just to get access to Kevin.
jokes.punchline: Darryl, the seasoned veteran, graciously concedes the point: 'See you next year, sport' — as if this is a professional rivalry.
jokes.explanation: Darryl treating the Girl Scout cookie territory conflict as a high-stakes professional game is consistently funny. 'See you next year, sport' gives Toby unexpected competence while maintaining the absurd stakes.

jokes.text: 'Metaphorically sixty-nined.' 'Ew! Perverts.' 'No offense, Oscar.'
jokes.setup: Kevin said he wanted to be 'sixty-nined'; people react with disgust.
jokes.punchline: Kevin clarifies it's metaphorical (which makes it worse), then someone calls them perverts, then Kevin adds 'No offense, Oscar' — a completely unmotivated swipe at Oscar.
jokes.explanation: 'No offense, Oscar' as an unmotivated gay joke is the weakest part of this beat — it's a bit cheap. The 'metaphorically sixty-nined' clarification making it worse is the better part. Mixed bag.

jokes.text: Dwight's farewell to Jim: 'Jim, I just wanna say that we haven't always gotten along. And at times, I've even hated your guts. But...' [long pause, emotional buildup] 'Bye-bye. I win.'
jokes.setup: Dwight appears to be setting up a heartfelt, emotional farewell to Jim.
jokes.punchline: 'Bye-bye. I win.' — Dwight abandons any sentimentality, declares victory, and leaves.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode and arguably in the Dwight/Jim relationship's history. The setup is perfect — all the signifiers of an emotional sitcom goodbye (pause, 'I just wanna say,' acknowledgment of conflict) — and then 'Bye-bye. I win.' collapses it completely. It's pure Dwight: competitive to the very end, incapable of sentimentality, and yet the 'I win' somehow captures the whole relationship. The pause before the punchline is doing enormous structural work. Very high quotability and character integration.

jokes.text: Jim's talking head: 'Well, he's Florida's problem now.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just left; Jim delivers a farewell confessional.
jokes.punchline: 'He's Florida's problem now' — Jim's total emotional deflation, treating Dwight like a burden being passed to another jurisdiction.
jokes.explanation: Short, devastating, and very Jim. The framing of Dwight as a regional liability being transferred is perfect. Very high economy — five words do the full job. Highly quotable and completely in character.

jokes.text: Robert: 'The Sabre store would work if we adopted the carnival model of leaving town once everyone's wise to us.'
jokes.setup: Robert is explaining to Jim why he's going to tank the Sabre store presentation despite publicly supporting it.
jokes.punchline: The 'carnival model of leaving town once everyone's wise to us' — a sardonic corporate metaphor that's also genuinely insightful about Sabre's product quality.
jokes.explanation: A very sharp line. Robert's cynical corporate worldview expressed through the 'carnival model' metaphor is both funny and cutting — it's the kind of line a genuinely witty person would say. High originality, economy, and character integration. Robert's erudite nihilism is perfectly captured. This is the kind of line you'd quote to explain the character.

jokes.text: Robert toasts Jim: 'Great job! Cheers.' — after explaining he liked the store but is going to deliberately tank it and get Dwight fired.
jokes.setup: Robert has just praised the Sabre store Jim helped create, then revealed he's going to kill it and possibly fire Dwight.
jokes.punchline: He gives Jim a warm 'Great job! Cheers' toast — completely sincere, no irony intended — which is more disturbing than if it were sarcastic.
jokes.explanation: Robert's cheerful compliment in the context of just describing his manipulative plan is darkly funny. His ability to separate praising someone from protecting them is chilling and comedic simultaneously. Works because James Spader plays it completely straight.

jokes.text: Robert: 'Shame, though -- I did like Dwight.' Then Dwight screaming 'I'm gonna win! Ha ha, I'm the gentleman! Suck it!' while racing Robert to the clubhouse.
jokes.setup: Robert just said he's going to tank the project and possibly fire Dwight, and notes he liked Dwight.
jokes.punchline: Cut to Dwight screaming 'I'm the gentleman! Suck it!' during a foot race — blissfully unaware of what's coming. Robert watches approvingly: 'Bravo, Dwight. Very good.'
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Robert's clinical 'I did like Dwight' with Dwight's triumphant obliviousness ('Suck it!') is great tonal comedy. Robert watching and saying 'Bravo, Dwight. Very good' with what sounds like genuine affection for a man he's about to destroy is darkly funny. The edit does a lot of the work here.

jokes.text: Presentation power move: 'Deeper market penetration, plus greater visibility, will raise Sabre—' 'To the power of two.' [synchronized spin move]
jokes.setup: Dwight is doing a rehearsed presentation with Robert, complete with choreographed spin moves.
jokes.punchline: The synchronized corporate-speak with physical flourish ('to the power of two' + spin) is treated with deadly seriousness by both, making it absurd.
jokes.explanation: The choreographed corporate-presentation schtick is mildly funny — the spectacle of Dwight and Robert doing synchronized moves is absurd. Less funny on paper than in execution.

jokes.text: Todd Packer asks to join the presentation spin: 'When you guys do that whole "power of two" shebang, how about I pop up also? I guess we'd have to say "power of three."' Robert: 'That is a great idea. Cathy, write that down and print it out. It's gonna make some really good toilet paper.'
jokes.setup: Todd Packer ingratiates himself, suggesting he join the choreographed presentation bit.
jokes.punchline: Robert California appears to agree enthusiastically, then immediately destroys it: 'It's gonna make some really good toilet paper.'
jokes.explanation: Robert's devastating dismissal of Todd is a great burn — the false setup (appearing to agree) followed by 'it's gonna make some really good toilet paper' is a well-constructed two-beat takedown. Very Robert: he won't say 'no,' he says yes and then eviscerates you. High character integration.

jokes.text: 'Cathy, write that down and print it out. It's gonna make some really good toilet paper.'
jokes.setup: Someone has suggested Todd Packer join the presentation
jokes.punchline: Dwight sarcastically asks Cathy to document it 'for toilet paper' — his contempt for Packer expressed as bureaucratic snark
jokes.explanation: Functional insult comedy — using Cathy as a recorder for a message of contempt is slightly bureaucratic-funny. Not Dwight's sharpest moment but in character.

jokes.text: Andy dismissing Jim with rapid-fire insults: 'What, your stylist ran out of messy spray?' / 'your face does look like the guy from Operation' / 'You look like the world's tallest hobbit.'
jokes.setup: Jim tries to warn Andy about something important; Andy refuses to listen and escalates to personal insults.
jokes.punchline: Each Jim interruption is met with a new, increasingly creative insult: 'Wooly Willie,' 'guy from Operation,' 'world's tallest hobbit.'
jokes.explanation: The escalating insult list is entertaining — each one is specific and oddly creative. 'World's tallest hobbit' is the best of the three. The 'that's the same guy' / 'different guy' meta-argument about Wooly Willie and Operation guy is a nice bonus gag within the gag.

jokes.text: Mini-argument about whether Wooly Willie and the Operation guy are the same: 'That's the joke I made.' 'That's not--' 'Different guy.'
jokes.setup: Andy says Jim looks like the guy from Operation; someone notes that's the same as the Wooly Willie joke Andy made.
jokes.punchline: Andy insists they're different guys — the absurdity of defending the distinction between two fictional men who may or may not exist.
jokes.explanation: A bonus gag embedded in the insult escalation. Andy doubling down on 'different guy' while Jim tries to move on is a nice secondary layer. Quick and efficient.

jokes.text: Erin trying to video chat Andy: 'Can you help me? I'm trying to make a video chat with Andy.' Jim: 'You don't "make a video chat" — you "video chat."'
jokes.setup: Erin asks Jim for help with video chat technology.
jokes.punchline: Jim's correction of her phrasing — 'you don't "make a video chat"' — is the kind of pedantic correction that reveals both Jim's mild superiority and Erin's lovable tech confusion.
jokes.explanation: Mild, functional joke. Jim's grammar correction is in character and Erin's tech innocence is well-established. Not especially creative but lands as a light beat.

jokes.text: Erin reveals her password is 'Erin123' — Jim: 'That's a terrible password.'
jokes.setup: Jim helps Erin with her laptop; she types her password.
jokes.punchline: 'Erin123' — her name plus sequential numbers — and Jim's flat judgment: 'That's a terrible password.'
jokes.explanation: A quick gag that characterizes Erin's innocence well. Not original (password jokes are common) but the character integration is solid. Jim's flat delivery of 'That's a terrible password' is the only funny part.

jokes.text: Video chat visual gag: Erin and Andy's video connection keeps breaking — 'There's something wrong with my laptop. Oh! I fixed it.' [Andy's screen goes black] 'Oh! Now mine's broken. Hang on.'
jokes.setup: Erin is trying to have a meaningful video call with Andy from Florida; the connection is unstable.
jokes.punchline: Every time one fixes the connection, the other's breaks — the technology actively resisting their emotional conversation.
jokes.explanation: Functional visual/tech comedy that also serves the emotional plot (the connection problems mirror their emotional disconnect). Not particularly original — technology-failing-at-emotional-moment is a well-worn comedic device. Works fine but doesn't transcend.

jokes.text: Andy reacts to Erin announcing she's not coming back: 'Yeah, that's awesome. That's great.' Then he plays a sad breakup song on his ukulele.
jokes.setup: Erin tells Andy over video chat that she's staying in Florida permanently.
jokes.punchline: Andy's forced, hollow 'Yeah, that's awesome. That's great' — followed by what we can infer is him playing sad music — is tragicomic.
jokes.explanation: Andy's 'that's awesome' when clearly devastated is a well-worn character beat for him — he performs enthusiasm to mask hurt. The ukulele song adds a sad-funny layer. Functional emotional comedy.

jokes.text: Andy plays '♪ Oh, baby, telephone / and tell me I'm your own ♪' on ukulele after Erin says she's not coming back.
jokes.setup: Andy is processing Erin's announcement that she's staying in Florida.
jokes.punchline: He performs a plaintive love song on the ukulele, completely earnestly, as if the song might somehow help.
jokes.explanation: Andy's musical response to emotional pain is well-established character comedy. The specific song choice and earnestness makes it more cringe than funny, which is appropriate. Works as character moment but not a stand-alone joke.

jokes.text: Jim: 'He said "I did like Dwight"? He's gonna fire him.' Office Worker: 'No, no, I think it was more like... "I liked him, but I don't any more, 'cause he did a bad job. So I'm definitely gonna yell at him."' Jim: 'Robert doesn't talk like that.'
jokes.setup: Jim tells the Scranton office about Robert's ominous 'I did like Dwight' comment.
jokes.punchline: Oscar's hilariously clunky, un-Robert-like paraphrase ('I'm definitely gonna yell at him') and Jim's flat 'Robert doesn't talk like that.'
jokes.explanation: Oscar's attempt to normalize Robert California's ominous language by translating it into plain speech is funny — the translation is so clunky it proves Jim's point. 'Robert doesn't talk like that' is the perfect button. Good character insight into both Robert and Oscar.

jokes.text: 'Look, you haven't dealt with him in a while, all right? He's like Super Dwight. It's like he's been bitten by a radioactive Dwight or som--'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to explain why he couldn't get through to Dwight to Oscar.
jokes.punchline: 'He's been bitten by a radioactive Dwight' — Jim's Spider-Man metaphor for Dwight at peak intensity, cut off mid-sentence.
jokes.explanation: A very quotable Jim line. 'Bitten by a radioactive Dwight' is an inspired metaphor — it exactly captures what it would mean to have all of Dwight's qualities amplified, and applying a superhero origin story to Dwight-at-peak is genuinely clever. The cut-off makes it feel natural and improvised. High quotability and character integration.

jokes.text: Stanley reacting to being consulted: 'Don't talk to me.' Then: 'Stanley's very upset that we're leaving Florida.'
jokes.setup: Jim turns to Stanley for backup in his argument.
jokes.punchline: 'Don't talk to me.' — Stanley's complete disengagement, explained by the fact that he's upset they're leaving his vacation paradise.
jokes.explanation: Classic Stanley — complete refusal to engage with office drama. 'Don't talk to me' does everything needed in four words. The explanation (he's upset about leaving Florida) adds a nice character-consistent layer. Very Stanley, very efficient.

jokes.text: Cookie war deliberations: Kevin suggests Darryl sing the frog song from Looney Tunes, 'Make them kiss each other. Make them kiss me! Eww.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is deliberating over who to buy cookies from and extracting maximum entertainment value.
jokes.punchline: His escalating demands end with 'Make them kiss me!' — Kevin treating the situation as his personal entertainment show.
jokes.explanation: Kevin's expanding list of demands culminating in 'Make them kiss me!' is funny — it's absurd but also perfectly Kevin, who sees himself as a desirable prize. The 'Eww' reaction from others is a nice beat.

jokes.text: 'What's a skinny guy like Toby know about cookies? You can't trust him to understand the wants and needs of the thick man. Maybe Toby from two years ago.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is adjudicating the cookie-selling dispute between Darryl and Toby
jokes.punchline: Kevin frames the dispute in terms of body size representation — 'the wants and needs of the thick man' — positioning himself as an advocate for large people's cookie interests, with the added jab that even Toby's past self doesn't qualify
jokes.explanation: Kevin at his absolute best. 'The wants and needs of the thick man' is a genuinely brilliant construction — Kevin has created a political identity around large cookie consumers and is speaking as their representative. The 'Maybe Toby from two years ago' tag implies Kevin has been tracking Toby's weight for years specifically to assess his cookie-market credibility. Complete character integration: only Kevin thinks in these terms and says them with complete seriousness. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Kevin video-chatting with Erin about her tan: 'I want you looking totally puertoriquena when I see you.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is inspecting Erin's tan via video chat, debating whether a spot is a tan or freckle.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's unsolicited aesthetic demand that Erin look 'totally puertoriquena' — bizarre, inappropriate, and delivered with total sincerity.
jokes.explanation: This joke is the weakest of the Kevin material — it relies on racial awkwardness without a clear comedic payoff, and Kevin's obliviousness doesn't quite elevate it. The 'inspect the tan in person' beat is slightly creepy without being funny-creepy. Below-average execution.

jokes.text: Cookie competition escalation: Kevin's hunger level negotiations — '40 boxes?' / 'Hungrier.' / '50?' / 'Hungrier.' / 'Triple digits.'
jokes.setup: Darryl and Toby are trying to win Kevin's business; Kevin keeps escalating his hunger
jokes.punchline: 'Triple digits' — Kevin plans to buy over 100 boxes of cookies, which is both absurd and completely believable for Kevin
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation structure. The Darryl/Toby guesses getting progressively higher while Kevin keeps saying 'hungrier' is a beautiful comedic rhythm. 'Triple digits' as the reveal is perfect — it's both shocking (100+ boxes?) and completely on-brand for Kevin. The implication that Kevin can eat triple-digit boxes of cookies is a dark and funny extension of the 'relatively thin man' setup earlier.

jokes.text: Dwight dismisses Jim again: 'Gosh, I keep throwing you away, you keep flying back. You're like an amish return-stick.'
jokes.setup: Jim appears again to warn Dwight; Dwight has already dismissed him multiple times.
jokes.punchline: 'You're like an amish return-stick' — Dwight's version of calling Jim a boomerang, filtered through his rural Germanic sensibility.
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best lines. 'Amish return-stick' is a completely original Dwight-specific insult — it's his version of 'boomerang' filtered through his Schrute Farms/Pennsylvania Dutch worldview. The specificity is what makes it exceptional: no other character on any other show would say 'amish return-stick.' Very high originality and character integration. Extremely quotable. The construction ('I keep throwing you away, you keep flying back') is also well-structured before the payoff.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'Wait, do you wanna borrow money?' — interpreting Jim's desperate 'I need to tell you one thing' as a request for a loan.
jokes.setup: Jim desperately tries to get Dwight to listen; Dwight agrees to hear one thing.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's instant assumption is that Jim wants money — revealing what Dwight thinks Jim's problems are.
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat — Dwight's assumption that Jim needs money is both dismissive and reveals Dwight's framework for 'problems.' Efficient one-liner that works in context.

jokes.text: Dwight dismisses Jim's warning: 'Your pranks have never worked in the past, and they're not gonna work today.' Jim: 'Okay, first of all, they've mostly worked.'
jokes.setup: Dwight dismisses Jim's warning about Robert as 'a prank.'
jokes.punchline: Jim's gentle correction — 'they've mostly worked' — is an acknowledgment of the entire Dwight/Jim prank history within the show.
jokes.explanation: A lovely meta-joke for fans of the show — 'they've mostly worked' is Jim gently setting the record straight on eight seasons of pranks. It's delivered with exactly the right level of casual confidence. High character integration and very rewarding for long-time viewers.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'You might wanna get to the airport. It's gonna take you a long time to get through security with all those beauty products.'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to warn Dwight; Dwight dismisses him one final time.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's goodbye insult implies Jim is excessively groomed — a dig that also reveals Dwight's contempt for vanity.
jokes.explanation: A competent Dwight insult but not especially creative. Echoes Andy's earlier 'messy spray' line, which makes it feel slightly repetitive. Functional.

jokes.text: Dwight's triumphant monologue: 'Nothing is gonna stop me. That is the mark of a great man-- Unstoppability. Dunder Mifflin... the farm, Mose. All those things. Vanish in my rearview mirror. Now if you'll excuse me, I have a date with destiny. And from what I hear, she's a-- Oh!'
jokes.setup: Dwight delivers a grand monologue about his destiny and unstoppability.
jokes.punchline: 'And from what I hear, she's a—' — cut off by what is implied to be Dwight hurting himself/tripping (the 'Oh!'), deflating the entire speech.
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedic structure. Dwight builds to a grandiose flourish — 'I have a date with destiny, and from what I hear, she's a—' — and is immediately cut off by physical comedy. The pomposity-deflated-by-pratfall structure is a classic, but it's perfectly timed and the specific windup is very Dwight. The 'Unstoppability' coinage and the solemn farewell to Mose are also funny within the monologue.

jokes.text: Jim pretends to bite Dwight to stop him, then accidentally hits Dwight's appendix wound: 'Oh, gross! Don't lick my hand! God, why is there so much saliva?' / 'All I had to do was think about pie, and my salivary glands did the rest.'
jokes.setup: Jim physically tries to stop Dwight from entering the presentation.
jokes.punchline: Jim licks/bites Dwight's hand to stop him; Dwight is indignant about the excessive saliva but explains it by revealing he was thinking about pie.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'Jim tries to stop Dwight' to 'Jim has to lick his hand' is absurd and physical. But the real joke is Dwight's explanation: 'All I had to do was think about pie, and my salivary glands did the rest' — delivered as useful information, not embarrassment. Very Dwight. The appendix wound callback adds a layer.

jokes.text: Dwight clutches his appendix wound: 'Oh, my appendix. My wound hasn't healed yet.' Jim: 'I'm sorry.' — repeated apologizing as Dwight writhes.
jokes.setup: Jim accidentally hits Dwight's appendix scar while trying to stop him.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's immediate collapse from unstoppable force to writhing in pain — from grandiosity to vulnerability in one touch.
jokes.explanation: The physical deflation of Dwight's monologue moment is well-timed — the 'unstoppable man' stopped by his own appendix wound is good irony. Works as a callback. Not particularly original on its own but effective in context.

jokes.text: Todd Packer steps in to replace missing Dwight: 'Oh, look like shnoot's a no-show. Guess he wasn't Vice President material after all. But I am. Put me in, babe. I've got the info down backwards, forwards, and doggy-style.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is missing from the presentation; Robert needs someone to step in.
jokes.punchline: Todd Packer immediately volunteers, pitching himself with 'I've got the info down backwards, forwards, and doggy-style.'
jokes.explanation: Classic Todd Packer — inappropriate sexual reference in a professional context ('doggy-style'), complete with the smugness of someone who thinks this is charming. The 'shnoot' is a good Packer-ism. Character-consistent but not particularly inventive.

jokes.text: Todd Packer is introduced as Vice President: '...allow me to introduce the Vice President of Sabre retail — Mr. Todd Packer.' [pause] ''Sup?'
jokes.setup: A formal board presentation. Robert builds to a grand introduction of the Vice President of Sabre retail.
jokes.punchline: Todd Packer's response to being formally introduced to a corporate board is ''Sup?'
jokes.explanation: The economy here is exceptional — the entire joke is one word: ''Sup?' The formal buildup (Robert's ceremonial introduction, the board setting) against the absolute nadir of professional greetings is perfectly structured. The pause before ''Sup?' makes the room feel the silence. Very high character integration: Todd Packer would absolutely say this.

jokes.text: Ryan tells Kelly he updated his Tumblr to announce Erin's departure: 'Ryan, why didn't you tell me?' 'Thought you checked my Tumblr.' 'You never update it.' 'Well, I updated it.'
jokes.setup: Phyllis is upset nobody told her Erin wasn't coming back.
jokes.punchline: Ryan's expectation that people monitor his Tumblr for company announcements — and Kelly's confirmation that he 'never updates it' — reveals Ryan's social media delusion.
jokes.explanation: Ryan's Tumblr as official company communication is a great piece of Ryan character comedy — his tech-bro self-importance applied to the most mundane situations. Kelly's 'you never update it' grounds the joke in reality.

jokes.text: Jim tries to stop Dwight by blocking his path: 'I'm not gonna let you by.' Dwight: 'Then you know what? I'm gonna have to run right through you.' Jim: 'Okay.' Dwight revs up. Jim: 'Are you really revving up? You know that doesn't work.' 'Jackie Chan!'
jokes.setup: Jim physically blocks Dwight's path to the presentation.
jokes.punchline: Dwight 'revs up' to charge through Jim, Jim patiently points out this doesn't work, and Dwight shouts 'Jackie Chan!' as a battle cry before charging.
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy here is excellent in context. Jim's patient deconstruction of Dwight's 'revving up' ('You know that doesn't work') is great — he's been here before. But 'Jackie Chan!' as a battle cry is inspired and very Dwight. The matter-of-fact physical confrontation between these two is consistently funny and character-defining.

jokes.text: Jim tries to physically block Dwight from entering the presentation: running battle with Dwight trying to run through Jim, revving up, 'Jackie Chan!'
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to physically stop Dwight from walking into his own firing
jokes.punchline: Dwight 'revs up' to run through Jim (Jim notes 'you know that doesn't work'), then attempts a 'Jackie Chan' move — treating a workplace corridor like an action movie
jokes.explanation: Good physical comedy sequence. 'You know that doesn't work' implies this is a known Dwight behavior — he's attempted the rev-up before. 'Jackie Chan!' as a battle cry while attempting a martial arts move in the lobby is peak Dwight physical comedy.

jokes.text: Kevin's voicemail: 'Hi, this is Alex. And this is Sam. Kevin can't come to the phone right now because he's busy... With us.' Kevin (pleased): 'Perfect! Now people will think I'm doing hot girls all day.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has apparently enlisted two women (Darryl and Toby doing voices? Or actual girls) to record his voicemail.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's delighted conclusion: 'Now people will think I'm doing hot girls all day' — his reputation management strategy.
jokes.explanation: Kevin's social strategy — get 'Alex' and 'Sam' to record his voicemail to imply he's with women — is funny because it's both pathetic and logical in Kevin's framework. The immediate concern that 'Alex' and 'Sam' sound like guy names adds a nice bonus layer.

jokes.text: 'I don't know, man, they might think we're drag queens.' 'Yeah, I don't know why you picked names that are also guys' names.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is pleased with his 'hot girls' voicemail; his collaborators raise concerns.
jokes.punchline: The practical critique — the names 'Alex' and 'Sam' are ambiguous — undercuts the entire scheme.
jokes.explanation: The logical deconstruction of Kevin's plan via the gendered-names problem is a nice bonus beat. 'They might think we're drag queens' is the better of the two lines — specific and funny.

jokes.text: Kevin demands: 'Now who do I ride to the kitchen like a pony?' Darryl: 'Don't make me be your pony, Kevin.' Toby: 'I refuse to be another man's horsey.'
jokes.setup: Kevin has been extracting increasingly humiliating demands from Darryl and Toby in exchange for buying their cookies.
jokes.punchline: The pony ride demand — Toby's dignified 'I refuse to be another man's horsey' being particularly funny.
jokes.explanation: 'I refuse to be another man's horsey' is the best line of the cookie subplot — Toby stating this with quiet dignity is perfectly in character and funnier than the demand itself. The 'another man's' implies this has happened before, which is an extra layer.

jokes.text: Kevin announces: 'I'll do anything!' Then sings the Michigan J. Frog song ('Hello, my baby, hello, my honey...') to Darryl and Toby.
jokes.setup: Darryl and Toby threaten to leave the cookie competition over Kevin's pony demand.
jokes.punchline: Kevin, desperate, reverses the situation — now HE is performing for THEM, singing the Looney Tunes frog song he himself demanded they sing for him.
jokes.explanation: The reversal is the joke — Kevin went from demanding others perform for him to performing the exact song he demanded. The structural callback is well-executed. Kevin singing the Michigan J. Frog song with full commitment is inherently funny and very Kevin.

jokes.text: 'I'm even gonna kiss Meredith.' [Kiss] 'That is -- Hmm. That's... so good.'
jokes.setup: Kevin announces he'll do anything to sell cookies, including kissing Meredith.
jokes.punchline: He kisses Meredith and seems genuinely pleased: 'That's... so good.' — as if discovering something unexpected.
jokes.explanation: The joke has two parts: Kevin offering to kiss Meredith as a 'sacrifice' (cringe), and then finding he actually likes it (escalating cringe into something weirder). 'That's... so good' with the pause is the better part — it reveals Kevin's suppressed attraction to Meredith, which is funnier than the kiss itself.

jokes.text: 'Thunderslam!' — Dwight body-slams Jim to get past him, Jim crashes.
jokes.setup: Jim is blocking Dwight's path; Dwight has run out of other options.
jokes.punchline: Dwight announces and executes a 'Thunderslam' — a named wrestling move — on Jim.
jokes.explanation: The naming of the move — 'Thunderslam!' — is the joke. Dwight doesn't just body-slam Jim; he announces it with a named technique. This is perfectly Dwight: treating a hallway altercation with the ceremony of a wrestling match. Very high character integration and quotability. The word itself ('Thunderslam') is inherently funny.

jokes.text: Dwight vs. Jim physical confrontation: 'No! This will end now.' / 'Thunderslam!' — Dwight performs a wrestling move on Jim, Jim is temporarily incapacitated
jokes.setup: Jim is trying to stop Dwight from entering the presentation room
jokes.punchline: Dwight names and executes a wrestling move called the 'Thunderslam' to break free
jokes.explanation: The 'Thunderslam' is a Dwight-specific joy — he has named wrestling moves, because of course he has. The fact that he names it before executing it (announcing his attack like a pro wrestler) is perfect Dwight. Maximum character integration: Dwight Schrute is exactly the kind of person who has practiced named wrestling moves and waits for the right moment to deploy them. Highly quotable fan moment.

jokes.text: Aftermath of Thunderslam: 'Anything else you need to talk about?' 'Nope. That was it.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has just body-slammed Jim into a wall/floor.
jokes.punchline: Both parties treat it with complete professional normalcy — Jim confirms that was all, Dwight confirms it's handled.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan aftermath is as funny as the Thunderslam itself. 'Anything else you need to talk about?' 'Nope. That was it.' treats a physical assault as a minor agenda item. The extreme economy — ten words — does maximum comedic work. Very high economy score; strong character work from both.

jokes.text: Robert's presentation takedown of the Sabre store begins with 'What baffles me is how you could take a perfectly good idea... and then utterly botch it in execution.' Todd Packer responds: 'If I may speak to that, I have only been Vice President of this project for the last half hour. So the man you want is Dwight Schrute.'
jokes.setup: Robert begins systematically destroying the Sabre store in his presentation.
jokes.punchline: Todd Packer, who just got the job 30 minutes ago, immediately and shamelessly throws Dwight under the bus with impeccable corporate logic.
jokes.explanation: Todd Packer's survival instinct in throwing Dwight under the bus — with the specific detail of 'the last half hour' — is very funny because it's technically accurate and completely shameless. The corporate logic is airtight even as it's morally bankrupt.

jokes.text: Robert's presentation ambush: 'What baffles me is how you could take a perfectly good idea, which the great Jo Bennett rightfully signed off on, and then utterly botch it in execution.'
jokes.setup: The board presentation begins; everyone expects Robert to support the store
jokes.punchline: Robert immediately attacks the project he himself has been pretending to champion — the whiplash is the joke, and the specific invocation of 'the great Jo Bennett' to deflect blame is a masterful corporate maneuver played for laughs
jokes.explanation: Robert California's corporate sociopathy on display — praising Jo Bennett's wisdom while using it as a shield to attack the very project Jo endorsed. The word 'baffles' is doing a lot of work as a performative expression of confusion he doesn't actually feel. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Dwight arrives late and immediately throws Todd Packer under the bus: 'I have only been Vice President of this project for the last half hour. So the man you want is Dwight Schrute.' / 'I don't see Dwight.' / 'He clearly had the infinite wisdom to stay as far away from this clown show as possible.'
jokes.setup: Todd Packer has been warming the VP seat and is now being attacked in the presentation
jokes.punchline: Packer immediately deflects to Dwight ('the man you want is Dwight Schrute'), but Dwight's not there — leading Robert to conclude Dwight 'had the wisdom' to avoid this mess
jokes.explanation: Nice irony — Dwight's absence (caused by Jim's intervention) makes him look good in the very meeting that was supposed to destroy him. 'He clearly had the infinite wisdom to stay as far away from this clown show as possible' is Robert at his most acidly funny.

jokes.text: Robert's speech defending Todd Packer from himself: 'Whatever you do... Do not blame Todd Packer. It is not his fault. Blame his upbringing, his parents. The society that would mold this idiotic creature. Fire the employee, yes. But not the man. You may not cancel his soul.'
jokes.setup: Robert is delivering his presentation verdict on the Sabre store failure. It's unclear if he's defending or condemning Packer.
jokes.punchline: Robert's defense of Todd escalates into philosophical absurdity — 'the society that would mold this idiotic creature' / 'You may not cancel his soul' — while firing him.
jokes.explanation: This is among the best Robert California moments. The philosophical defense-while-firing is vintage Robert: 'the society that would mold this idiotic creature' is both an insult and a defense in the same breath. 'You may not cancel his soul' is a legitimately brilliant line — absurd, grandiose, and perfectly Robert. The structure (appears to be defending, reveals he's firing) is well-executed. Very high character integration and originality.

jokes.text: Robert's defense of Packer: 'Whatever you do... do not blame Todd Packer... Blame his upbringing, his parents. The society that would mold this idiotic creature. Fire the employee, yes. But not the man. You may not cancel his soul.'
jokes.setup: Robert is ostensibly defending Todd Packer from board criticism
jokes.punchline: The defense escalates into existential philosophy — 'You may not cancel his soul' — while simultaneously confirming Packer is an 'idiotic creature' and should absolutely be fired
jokes.explanation: One of the best Robert California moments in the series. The speech is structured as a defense but functions as a prosecution — every sentence supposedly defending Packer actually confirms he's terrible. 'The society that would mold this idiotic creature' is simultaneously empathetic and devastating. 'You may not cancel his soul' is Robert California's operatic grandiosity at its peak. This could be on a highlights reel. Maximum character integration — this speech only works from James Spader's character. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Robert: 'And yet, Todd, it's you who's fired.' Todd: 'What-- I can't get fired. I'm an institution. I have been at this company for 20 years. How many of you have been here that long, huh?'
jokes.setup: Robert has been building to something; Todd thinks he's been defended.
jokes.punchline: Todd is fired. His defense — 'I'm an institution' / '20 years' — is the most he's ever claimed professional legitimacy, which makes it funnier given his behavior.
jokes.explanation: The firing is well-executed, but the bigger joke is Robert's speech (Joke #68). Packer's 'I'm an institution' defense is character-appropriate but not especially creative. The moment lands primarily on the strength of the setup.

jokes.text: Dwight returns to Scranton with Jim: 'Hey, Dwight, what are you doing here? I thought you were supposed to be in Florida.' 'Yeah, the crazy thing about that is, um-- Wow, you look great. Did you lose some weight?'
jokes.setup: The Scranton office is surprised to see Dwight back; Phyllis asks what happened.
jokes.punchline: Dwight completely deflects the question with a compliment — 'Did you lose some weight?' — rather than explain his professional humiliation.
jokes.explanation: Dwight's abrupt subject change to complimenting Phyllis rather than explaining his failed Florida venture is good character comedy — his pride cannot allow him to admit what happened. The specific choice of 'did you lose some weight?' is also funny because Dwight would only say this strategically.

jokes.text: Jim and Pam reunion: 'Hey, stranger!' 'Hey!' 'Oh, I missed you.' 'I missed you.'
jokes.setup: Jim returns to Scranton after the Florida trip.
jokes.punchline: The warm reunion plays straight — but in context of this episode's earlier 'Sweet' joke about Dwight leaving, Jim returning to Pam is the genuine emotional payoff that the episode earns as comedy-adjacent.
jokes.explanation: This is more emotional beat than joke. It's warm but not particularly funny. Included because it's a comedic-context beat in a comedy episode, but it doesn't generate laughs on its own.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head: 'I'm going to Florida to get Erin.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just been dumped (sort of) by Erin over video chat.
jokes.punchline: Andy's decisive declaration — 'I'm going to Florida to get Erin' — played as a grand romantic gesture, is undercut by how it's delivered as a mundane confessional.
jokes.explanation: The Andy-as-romantic-hero declaration is mildly funny given his track record. Functional cliffhanger beat with mild comedic value. The deadpan delivery of a dramatic decision is appropriately Office-style.

jokes.text: Andy's talking head spirals: 'I forgot to check my email. It's crazy, right? It's just, when she said she was leaving... I thought... You're about to close four tabs, are you sure you want to continue? Yes. I am sure. Ahh! Slow computer!'
jokes.setup: Andy is delivering what should be an emotional talking head about deciding to pursue Erin.
jokes.punchline: The confessional completely derails as Andy gets frustrated with his computer — 'Ahh! Slow computer!' — breaking the emotional moment with mundane tech irritation.
jokes.explanation: A very funny episode-closing joke. Andy's big emotional declaration is completely sabotaged by his own computer frustration — the 'four tabs' warning and 'Slow computer!' undercut the romance perfectly. It's also very Andy: he can't sustain emotional gravity. The computer-dialog interrupting his thoughts is a clever structural choice.

tmdb_overview: Jim comes to Dwight's rescue when Robert slams the plan for the Sabre Store concept. Andy discovers Erin doesn't plan to return to Scranton.
